channel.title: Selected papers | Quantum Research Center
channel.description: Recent arXiv papers in quantum foundations, computing, and information, with explanations of their transferable methods.

item.title: Certification Time for Weak-Force-Mediated Entanglement between Levitated Particles
item.description:
Experiments with levitated nanoparticles aim to show that a weak force, and eventually gravity, entangles the motion of two particles. Producing the entangled state is only half the task: it has to be told apart from separable states using a finite number of noisy measurements, taken one run at a time. How many measurements, and how much laboratory time, does certification need, and which protocol reaches the weakest forces? For a two-mode Gaussian state with smallest partially transposed symplectic eigenvalue 	ilde
u_-<1, certification at z standard deviations needs about N_\star=(z\alpha/(1-	ilde
u_-))^2 measurements. With isotropic readout noise \xi, \alpha\ge	ilde
u_-+\xi, with equality for symmetric thermal two-mode squeezed states, while local squeezing leaves the entanglement unchanged and makes \alpha arbitrarily large. In release–recapture, at a fixed ratio of diffusion to coupling, the entanglement stays finite as the force weakens but N_\star grows as 1/g and the total time as g^{-3/2}. Release–recapture certifies entanglement at couplings orders of magnitude weaker than continuous monitoring, and the release time that certifies fastest is longer than the one that entangles most.

item.title: Qubit-environment entanglement in pure dephasing dynamics for mixed initial states
item.description: When a qubit only dephases, the joint qubit–environment state for a pure initial qubit is separable exactly when the environment ends up in the same state whichever pointer state the qubit is in, \hat R_{00}(t)=\hat R_{11}(t). This test made it possible to tell decoherence by entanglement from decoherence by classical correlations, and even to detect the difference on the qubit alone. Real qubits are already partly mixed. Does the test survive, and does entanglement then evolve as it does for pure qubits? If \hat R_{00}(t)=\hat R_{11}(t), the joint state stays separable, and zero-discord, for any initial qubit coherence. Otherwise, the family of minors that gave the pure-state criterion becomes only a witness: a negative minor proves entanglement, but nonnegative minors prove nothing. A Schur complement reduces the exact partial-transpose test to a matrix \hat D of the environment’s dimension, whose diagonal entries are those minors. Mixed qubits show behaviour impossible for pure ones: a separable initial period followed by sudden birth of entanglement, death and rebirth, and no entanglement at all during an entangling evolution when the qubit is strongly mixed. In a model of an NV-centre spin with up to five nuclear spins, the minors miss entanglement, sometimes for the whole evolution.

item.title: Meet-in-the-Middle Compilation of the [CNOT] Class with Fibonacci Anyons
item.description: Two qubits encoded in six Fibonacci anyons live in a five-dimensional fusion space, one dimension more than two qubits need. The only exchange that entangles the qubits, \sigma_3, is also the only one that couples them to the fifth, noncomputational state, so every entangling braid leaks. How small can the leakage of a braid equivalent to CNOT up to single-qubit gates be at a given length, and is exhaustive search better than random sampling? A GPU meet-in-the-middle search over all 5^{21} positive words finds at length 21 a braid with leakage \ell=3.95\times10^{-3} and distance 7.8\times10^{-9} to the CNOT class, less leakage than the best previously sampled braid of length 39. Restricting to \{\sigma_1,\sigma_2,\sigma_3\}, to words starting and ending with \sigma_3, to palindromes and to Garside normal forms extends exhaustive search to length 72; at length 69 it finds \ell=8.8\times10^{-11} with distance 4.3\times10^{-10}. The paper proves that leakage lies in \mathbb Z[\varphi] and that any nonzero leakage satisfies \ell\ge1/(1+C^{2L}) with C\approx2.89, and that for long random words the leakage distribution tends to \ell^{d-1}.

item.title: Quantum State Preparation for Complex-Valued Amplitudes
item.description: Quantum algorithms often compute numbers into binary registers with reversible arithmetic, but then need those numbers as amplitudes. For a complex z=x+iy, the usual route encodes x and y separately and adds them with a linear combination of unitaries, which fixes the normalisation by the ranges of x and y. How can z/\alpha be loaded coherently, for inputs in superposition, with a normalisation set by |z| itself? The procedure computes the magnitude r' and argument \phi' of z reversibly with CORDIC, which uses only shifts and additions. It then encodes r'/\alpha with an exact binary-to-amplitude routine, applies one phase gate per bit of \phi' to obtain e^{i\phi'}, and uncomputes the arithmetic. The cost is O(n^2) Toffoli and T gates and O(n) ancillas, with error |r'e^{i\phi'}-z|=O(2^{-(n-l)}) for n-bit inputs with l integer bits. A reversible in-place multiplication by 1+2^{-2j}, exactly invertible despite rounding, lets each CORDIC step run without storing an extra copy of a coordinate.

item.title: Prepare-and-measure quantum key distribution from a bound on information leakage
item.description: Every key distribution protocol has to limit what escapes the users’ laboratories. In a prepare-and-measure protocol this cannot be strict, since the source must send out a signal that depends on Alice’s private input. The minimal assumption is therefore a bound on how much the emitted systems, intended signal and side channels together, reveal about the input. Can that single number replace a model of the source’s states, dimension and energy, with nothing assumed about Bob’s measurement device? Yes, against collective attacks. The leakage bound states that the optimal number of correctly guessed inputs, out of n sent once each, is at most G, with G=2 meaning one bit. Statistics reproducible by a classical message within the same bound certify no key. This rules out all two-state protocols such as B92, and all matched-basis protocols such as BB84 and the six-state protocol. Tilting Bob’s measurements restores security: four qubit protocols certify one secret bit per key round in the ideal case, through a self-test on a virtual entanglement-based twin. With noise, the best tolerates visibility 0.838 (8.1% bit error rate) and the loss thresholds are \eta\ge0.764, about 1.2 dB. Numerically, the rates match the device-independent rates of the entanglement-based twins.

item.title: Matrix Samplers and Quantum-Proof Extractors: Their Correspondence and Almost-Optimal Constructions
item.description: To estimate the average of a bounded D\times D matrix-valued function in operator norm, O(\varepsilon^{-2}\log(2D/\delta)) independent samples suffice, but each costs m fresh random bits. Matrix samplers try to keep nearly that sample count while using only m+O(\log(D/\delta)) random bits. Classically, Zuckerman showed that averaging samplers and randomness extractors are the same objects. What kind of extractor is a matrix sampler, and can the correspondence give better constructions? A matrix sampler for D\times D matrices is the same thing as a seeded extractor whose output stays uniform against an adversary holding about \log(2D) qubits of side information, up to factor-two losses in the error. The paper then builds an explicit strong quantum-proof extractor with seed (1+\alpha)\log a+(2+\alpha)\log(1/\eta)+O_\alpha(1) and output n-O_\alpha(a+\log(1/\eta)) for sources of conditional min-entropy n-a. Through the correspondence, this gives explicit strong matrix samplers with m+O_\alpha(\log(D/\delta)) random bits and O_\alpha(\varepsilon^{-2-\alpha}\log^{1+\alpha}(D/\delta)) samples, replacing a polynomial dependence on D in earlier work by a logarithmic one. It also gives quantum-proof extractors with seed O(\log(n/\eta)) and output \Omega(n) for every constant entropy rate, where earlier constructions needed rate above one half.

item.title: Experimental evidence for quantum Brownian motion in electron-metal decoherence
item.description: Twenty years ago Anglin, Paz and Zurek proposed that an electron passing close to a metal loses coherence through quantum Brownian motion: its image charge dissipates energy in the metal, and by the fluctuation–dissipation theorem the same process randomizes the electron’s phase. Interferometer experiments near silicon found decoherence two orders of magnitude below the prediction, and those near gold were at the edge of detectability. Can electron–metal decoherence be measured and compared quantitatively with the theory? Yes, using a diffractometer instead of an interferometer. Diffracted 1.67 keV electrons enter a gold-plated microchannel at milliradian grazing incidence and bounce off the wall at sub-nanometre distance, which raises the interaction strength \Delta t/y^3 to about 10^7 ps/μm³. All diffraction orders broaden equally and fringe visibility falls to 30–60%. The measured decoherence rate peaks at 182 μm⁻² at a tilt of 4.6 mrad, close to the classical-trajectory prediction of 216 μm⁻², and a standing-wave model reproduces the turnover at small tilt with a fitted gold resistivity of 37\pm5 nΩ m.

item.title: Classical Verification of Quantum Computation Beyond the Polynomial Hierarchy
item.description: Can a classical polynomial-time verifier be convinced of the outcome of a quantum computation by the efficient quantum computer that ran it, with no cryptographic assumption? This is open for all of BQP, and every quantum problem known to have such a proof system lies in AM or was excluded only from MA relative to an oracle. Does efficient classical verification force a problem into the polynomial hierarchy? Not by any relativizing argument. Relative to a classical oracle, a variant of recursive Fourier sampling is decided exactly in quantum polynomial time, lies outside the polynomial hierarchy, and has a public-coin interactive proof with a classical verifier, an efficient quantum honest prover, perfect completeness and soundness error 1/4 against unbounded provers, using at most \log n/4 messages. The message count can be made to grow as slowly as any unbounded computable function, and for a suitable oracle it is optimal up to a constant factor.

item.title: Correlation-sensitive magic-state distillation from spin-squeezed neutral atoms
item.description: Magic-state distillation is analysed for independent noisy inputs, with a fidelity threshold above which each round improves the resource. Neutral-atom factories prepare many resource blocks in parallel under shared interactions and control fields, which correlates their errors. Can such correlations defeat distillation even when every input is above threshold, and which measurable quantity decides? Yes. For the five-to-one Bravyi–Kitaev protocol with independent local Clifford twirls, the accepted output depends on the joint input only through sums A_k of k-body correlators along the target axis: p_{\rm acc}=(3+A_4)/48 and t_{\rm out}=(A_3-2A_5)/(3+A_4). Distillation improves on the mean input exactly when G=A_3-2A_5-\bar t(3+A_4)>0. Inputs with identical one- and two-qubit reduced states can have opposite gains, and in finite-range Ising simulations of a 25-atom source, interblock correlations reverse the gain while the product of the same local states gains.

item.title: Measurement incompatibility and noiseless quantum codes
item.description: A quantum channel can destroy the incompatibility of measurements but never create it. Which channels preserve the incompatibility of every finite family of measurements? Chitambar and Zhang conjectured that, when the input is larger than the output, such a channel must carry a noiseless copy of its output space, and Uola and coauthors asked whether every dimension has a measurement family that is incompatible on the full space but compatible on every proper subspace. Both questions are settled. A channel from dimension D to d preserves all incompatibility if and only if an isometry W encodes every output state noiselessly, \mathcal N(W\rho W^\dagger)=\rho. One explicit family of d^2 binary measurements is a complete test: its compatibility threshold is s=1, and any channel that keeps that threshold has such a code. The same family is incompatible on \mathbb C^d and compatible on every proper subspace, for every d\ge2. If the threshold shifts by a small \delta, an approximate encoding has diamond-norm error at most 2c^2\delta^2.

item.title: Network nonlocality with tripartite entangled sources
item.description: Network nonlocality has mostly been studied with sources that emit pairs of particles. A three-qubit source has two distinct notions of nonlocality: the Mermin inequality excludes fully local models, and the Svetlichny inequality certifies genuine tripartite nonlocality. When independent sources emit three-qubit states and central nodes measure without any input, how is a network violation related to these two single-source tests? It depends on the wiring. In the closed network, where two input-free central nodes each hold one particle from every source, Bell-state measurements give a two-copy value at least the normalized Svetlichny value, \mathcal N_{\rm c}\ge\mathcal S/4; every entangled generalized GHZ state, and even some biseparable states, violate the network inequality. In the open network, with one central node, the value is at most the normalized Mermin value, \mathcal N_{\rm o}\le\mathcal M/2. With n sources, the largest violation of these two-correlator inequalities is \sqrt2 (closed) or 2 (open) for even n, but only 2^{1/2-1/(2n)} or 2^{1-1/(2n)} for odd n.

item.title: Many-body entanglement quantification in arbitrary states through a few partial-transpose moments
item.description: Logarithmic negativity quantifies entanglement in mixed states, but computing it needs the full spectrum of the partial transpose and hence tomography. Moments of the partial transpose can be measured with randomized measurements or swap circuits. Given a few such moments, what is the largest amount of negativity they certify? Treating the normalized squared eigenvalues of the partial transpose as a probability measure turns the question into a truncated Hausdorff moment problem, solved exactly by Gauss or Gauss–Radau quadrature. The moments p_2,\dots,p_K give the best possible lower bound \mathcal E_K. The bounds increase strictly until they become exact at K=4s, where s is the number of distinct eigenvalue magnitudes, and converge for every state. For K=4 the method reproduces the known bound \tfrac12\ln(p_2^3/p_4) and shows it is optimal.

item.title: Bargmann-invariant witness of the graviton commutator
item.description: Experiments proposed to show that gravity is quantum look for gravitationally induced entanglement or decoherence, but Newtonian entangling phases can be mimicked by assigning a classical field to each branch, and decoherence can be mimicked by classical noise. Is there an interference observable that no branchwise-definite classical gravitational field can reproduce? Yes. For matter coupled linearly to linearized gravity, each branch coherence factorizes exactly into a conservative phase, the characteristic functional of the graviton state, and a phase from the field commutator. For two interferometers, the phase \mathfrak B of a four-cycle Bargmann invariant cancels everything except the commutator: it is independent of the graviton state and of all Newtonian interactions, and it vanishes for every branchwise-definite classical model. It is bounded by which-path decoherence, \mathfrak B^2\le16\,\Gamma_X\Gamma_Y.

item.title: Self-Correcting 3D Surface Code with Growing Local Dimension
item.description: A self-correcting quantum memory keeps information for a time growing exponentially in a power of its size under local thermal dynamics, with no active correction. The 4D toric code achieves this, but in three dimensions a no-go theorem for fixed local dimension and the string-like logical operator of the 3D surface code stand in the way. Does allowing the local dimension q to grow with system size help? Yes. Changing only the Pauli powers of the 3D surface code along one axis, so that its string-like logical operator carries powers 1,2,4,\dots modulo q, gives a translation-invariant code in which, with odd q\ge cL^3 and below a critical temperature, both error sectors have memory time at least e^{\Omega(N^{1/3})} under single-qudit Metropolis dynamics. Numerics suggest \log t_{\rm mem}\sim\min\{q,N^{1/3}\}, so much smaller q may suffice.

item.title: Distillable entanglement is continuous
item.description: Distillable entanglement, the best rate at which copies of a state can be turned into Bell pairs by local operations and classical communication, is defined operationally and has no single-letter formula. It was known to be lower semicontinuous and continuous on the interior of distillable states, but not continuous in general. Is it continuous everywhere, with an explicit bound? Yes. For states within trace distance \varepsilon<1/16, |E_D(\rho)-E_D(\sigma)|\le4\sqrt\varepsilon\log d+4h(\sqrt\varepsilon), with d the smaller local dimension. The same bound holds for entanglement cost. The proof builds an explicit LOCC protocol that converts copies of \sigma into copies of \rho using a number of ebits per copy that vanishes as the states approach each other.

item.title: Quantum-enhanced metrology with classical shadows
item.description: Reaching the best precision in quantum metrology usually requires measuring a specific, often complicated observable tailored to the probe and encoding. Can one instead measure every qubit in random Pauli bases, as in classical shadows, and still estimate a parameter well, and how much entanglement advantage survives? Yes, with a quantified cost. Combining all Pauli moments up to weight K from one randomized data set by generalized least squares gives variance 1/(n\mathcal I), where the shadow information \mathcal I has a closed form. Separable probes reach at most \mathcal I=N/3, so exceeding it witnesses entanglement, and no probe exceeds 2N^2/(N+2)<2N. Entanglement therefore gives a constant-factor gain, at most 6, not Heisenberg scaling: about 15% for twisted probes of 12 qubits.

item.title: Exact Identification of Quantum Correlations in the Minimal Bell Scenario
item.description: In the simplest Bell experiment, two parties with two binary measurements each, the extreme points of the quantum set are known, but deciding whether a given list of eight statistics is quantum still requires searching over mixtures of many of them or climbing a semidefinite hierarchy that converges only in the limit. Is there an exact, finite test? Yes. A behaviour is quantum if and only if it is a mixture of a single behaviour produced by projective measurements on a pure two-qubit state and a local (classical) behaviour. The key step is a proof that every Bell functional with a strict quantum advantage has exactly one quantum maximizer. Membership then reduces to a system of trigonometric equations in five angles, and every quantum behaviour can be realized in dimension 6\times6.

item.title: Ancilla-free optimal quantum adder
item.description: Quantum addition sits inside factoring, discrete logarithms and many oracles. Ripple-carry adders need no extra qubits but have linear depth; carry-lookahead adders reach logarithmic depth only with extra workspace. Can an exact n-bit adder have O(n) gates and O(\log n) depth with no ancillary qubits at all? Yes. Using only X, CNOT and Toffoli gates with all-to-all connectivity, the paper builds an exact ancilla-free adder with O(n) gates and O(\log n) depth, which is optimal for both. A simpler recursive version achieves O(n\log\log n) gates at the same depth. The construction borrows existing control and data wires as dirty workspace and always restores them.

item.title: Finite Nonsignalling Resources Suffice to Simulate Entangled Qubits
item.description: One PR box (a binary-input nonsignalling resource) plus shared randomness reproduces all projective-measurement statistics of a maximally entangled qubit pair. Some partially entangled states cannot be simulated with one PR box, and every known exact protocol for them uses a box with real-valued inputs. Is a continuous input alphabet necessary, as Gisin asked? No. For every pure state \cos\theta|00\rangle+\sin\theta|11\rangle, shared randomness and at most K(\theta)=4\lceil\sqrt2\pi\cot^2\theta\rceil^2\le128\cot^4\theta PR boxes, used in parallel, reproduce all local projective statistics exactly, without communication or postselection. The budget does not depend on the measurement settings. The construction extends to every mixed two-qubit state and to all binary-outcome POVMs.

item.title: Certain Quantum States Already Require Quantum Time Evolution
item.description: Bell tests check quantum theory without assuming a model, but only its static structure. Could the dynamics be tested the same way? In phase-space theories where states are quasi-probability distributions and evolution is given by a generalized bracket, does the presence of certain states in the theory force the bracket to be the quantum (Moyal) one? Yes. Requiring that position and momentum marginals stay nonnegative under anharmonic evolution ties states to dynamics. If a particular superposition of the lowest three oscillator states is admissible, the bracket must be the Moyal bracket to all orders in \hbar^2. If only the first excited oscillator state is admissible, the leading correction must equal the quantum value a_1=-1/24. The ground state alone allows any a_1 between the classical value 0 and -1/24.

item.title: Elementary proofs of quantum lower bounds for element distinctness and k-sum
item.description: Element distinctness needs \Theta(n^{2/3}) quantum queries, but the known lower-bound proofs use the polynomial method, negative-weight adversaries or compressed oracles. The k-sum bound \Omega(n^{k/(k+1)}) needs the negative-weight adversary. Can these bounds be proved with basic linear algebra? Yes, in under two pages each. Refining the hybrid argument of Bennett, Bernstein, Brassard and Vazirani, the proof tracks second-order differences of algorithm states under changes to two input positions. This gives E\|\psi_T(y)-\psi_T(x)\|^2=O(T/n+T^3/n^2) between a distinct input and one with a planted collision, hence T=\Omega(n^{2/3}). With kth-order differences the same scheme gives \Omega(n^{k/(k+1)}) for k-sum over groups with |G|\ge n^k.

item.title: Entangled logical qubits on a superconducting quantum processor
item.description: On large superconducting chips, two effects not handled by standard surface-code circuits limit logical performance: leakage out of the qubit subspace and a fraction of underperforming qubits and couplers. Can a 120-qubit IBM processor with fast reset support logical memories, entangling operations and teleportation at useful fidelity? Yes. On ibm_phoenix, excluding bad components by re-purposing ancillas halves the distance-5 logical error per round from 1.9% to 0.9%, comparable to the best distance-3 patches. Lattice surgery between adjacent distance-3 codes gives logical Bell-state fidelity above 93%. Three logical qubits give state, Bell-pair and gate teleportation at 78–93%. A stability experiment with resets on every qubit every two rounds reaches about 2\times10^{-7} failure probability at 170 rounds.

item.title: One-sided-DIQKD using any pure bipartite entangled state secure against all attacks
item.description: In one-sided device-independent QKD, Bob’s measurements are trusted and Alice’s device is a black box, so security rests on quantum steering. Existing protocols use maximally entangled states, which are costly to make. Can every pure entangled state of any dimension yield a secret key in this setting, including with lossy detectors and noisy sources? Yes. In the noiseless case, self-testing of any pure state \sum_i\alpha_i|ii\rangle gives a key rate equal to its entanglement entropy. With depolarizing visibility \nu and efficiency \eta on Alice’s side, an entropic-uncertainty bound gives a closed-form rate that is affine in \eta, and hence a critical efficiency for every pure state and visibility. The critical efficiency is 1/2 for maximally entangled states and rises only slowly as entanglement falls.

item.title: Optimal probes for estimating the dephasing of a quantum spin system
item.description: To estimate the strength of dephasing on a spin J (or 2J qubits), which superposition of levels should be prepared? A spin cat state is optimal for weak Gaussian phase diffusion, but its coherence is the first to decay. Over what range does the cat stay optimal, and what works beyond it? For general dephasing channels, the QFI is concave in the probe populations and an ancilla never helps. The channel QFI is a second-order cone program whose dual variables are the optimal populations. For Gaussian diffusion the cat is globally optimal exactly for \Delta\le0.1424 at J=1 and \Delta\le0.065 at J=3/2; for larger J its range shrinks at least as 1/J^2. Beyond it, uniform superpositions, or a one-parameter interpolation between cat and uniform, are near optimal.

item.title: Local Dephasing Sustains Continuous Time Crystals in a Spin-1/2 Ensemble
item.description: Pure dephasing destroys single-spin coherence and is normally counted as loss. In a fully connected ferromagnetic spin-1/2 ensemble with local decay, can dephasing instead be what keeps a collective oscillation going, a continuous time crystal under time-independent dynamics? Yes. An exact operator identity shows that dephasing feeds energy into the transverse interaction, which local decay removes with a delay of order 1/\Gamma_1. In homogeneous mean field there is no periodic orbit without dephasing, and on a periodic orbit the delayed feedback exactly pays for the transverse damping. Liouvillian spectra for N=80–300 show oscillatory decay rates falling as N^{-0.32} and N^{-0.46}, with frequencies approaching the mean-field values.

item.title: Entanglement certification of attosecond light fields with photoelectron interferometry
item.description: High-harmonic generation is predicted to entangle the infrared driving field with extreme-ultraviolet harmonics. Standard optical certification needs local oscillators or photon-correlation detectors that barely exist at XUV frequencies. Can photoelectron interferometry (RABBIT), already routine in attosecond science, certify that entanglement on its own? Not from one sideband: every set of single-sideband moments has a fully separable explanation. Adding the two neighbouring sidebands supplies moments U and V, and |Q|^2>UV then certifies IR–XUV entanglement through the partial transpose. A further bound |Q|>H(U,V) certifies genuine three-mode entanglement and is tight when U=0. On model states, a displaced two-mode squeezed state is certified only in a window of displacement and squeezing, and a non-Gaussian GME family only for squeezing r<0.043.

item.title: The Impact of Markovian Errors on Random Circuits
item.description: Randomized benchmarking reports one error rate, but under gate-dependent noise it is unclear what that number measures. Average gate infidelity is gauge dependent, so it cannot be the answer. For small Markovian errors, how does each elementary error (Pauli-stochastic, over-rotation, axis tilt) enter the RB decay? For any gate set and sampling distribution forming a sequence-asymptotic unitary 2-design, Pauli-stochastic rates are the only errors that enter the decay linearly. Hamiltonian rates enter through a quadratic form that vanishes on gauge directions. For direct RB of \{X_{\pi/2},Y_{\pi/2}\} with probability p of X, the form is explicit in two over-rotations and one relative axis tilt. Equal over-rotations \theta give r=3\theta^2/4 at p=1/2, three times each gate’s infidelity, and about 16.6 times at p=0.9. For Clifford RB, a fixed form with weights 1/9 and 1/18 is filtered through the compilation.

item.title: Problem-aware sampling for bias and variance reduction in randomised Hamiltonian simulation
item.description: qDRIFT approximates e^{-iHT} by random Pauli rotations sampled in proportion to |c_j|, ignoring the initial state and the observable. Its estimators carry bias and variance that cost many steps and trajectories. When the goal is a single \langle O(T)\rangle from a known initial state, can the sampling distribution be tuned to the problem while keeping qDRIFT’s guarantees? Yes, with StateDRIFT. To fourth order in dt, bias and variance depend on the distribution only through a few t=0 quantities built from |\psi\rangle, O and the Hamiltonian terms. This gives closed-form variance-optimal rules, an interpolating family that provably improves both bias and variance at one step for sign-definite inputs, and an optimized family for deeper circuits. For molecules of 6 to 18 qubits the dynamics resolves in 1.7–26 times fewer steps and 1.2–11 times fewer two-qubit gates; for BeH_2 the gate count falls from 11,201 to 983. Mixing with 20% of the vanilla distribution bounds every reweighting by a factor of 5.

item.title: FVQKD: A Formal Verification of Quantum Key Distribution Security in Rocq
item.description: QKD security rests on hand-checked proofs that chain smooth entropies, an entropic uncertainty relation, a sampling bound and the leftover hash lemma, drawn from several papers with differing conventions. Can the composable finite-key security of BB84 be machine-checked end to end, from a formal protocol program to the key-length theorem? Yes, in FVQKD, a Rocq development of about 151,000 lines, 102,000 of them new, with no admitted lemmas and only the kernel plus three standard axioms. It proves composable finite-key security of BB84 at the tight Tomamichel et al. bound, for every initial state and every adversary channel acting on a formally specified protocol program. Mechanization exposed a missing case in the published argument: after conditioning on the test passing, the smoothing parameter \varepsilon/\sqrt{p_{\rm pass}} can exceed 1, outside the domain of the uncertainty relation. A second proof branch using the abort probability repairs it, and the key-length formula is unchanged. A concrete instance with n=k=10^4 certifies a 2000-bit key.

item.title: Reset-Enhanced Dissipative Quantum Metrology
item.description: Dissipation in open quantum sensors usually washes out parameter information. Can the simplest dissipative control, a channel that resets the probe to a fixed state at rate r, increase the quantum Fisher information in steady-state and transient sensing without changing the Hamiltonian or adding a coherent drive? Sometimes, and the paper says exactly when. An exact identity for \partial_rF gives a first-order test for local enhancement. For a thermal qubit reset to its ground state, steady-state thermometry improves if and only if 0<\beta\omega<\ln(2+\sqrt5) and r is below a threshold, with optimum r_{\rm opt}=\gamma(2+\sqrt5-e^{\beta\omega})/(e^{\beta\omega}-1). For diagonal dynamics, reset cannot change the leading short-time Fisher information of a static parameter, but it raises elapsed-time information immediately, roughly as r^2. For frequency estimation with reset to |+\rangle, the gain at t=1/\gamma is about 7 times, 91% of it from the coherence (eigenvector) part.
